chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Mahmoudi, from his father, from Yunus, from al-Husayn ibn Khalid, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I heard him (peace be upon him) saying: 'asws ) saying: 'It is obligatory upon the Imam ( 'asws ) when he sees a man committing adultery or drinking wine, that he establishes the Hadd (penalty) upon him, and he does not need proof along with his seeing, because he is the Trustee of Allah among His creation. And when he sees a man who steals, it is obligatory upon him to reprimand him, forbid him, and pass by leaving him.' I said, 'How is that so?' He ( 'asws ) said: 'Because the right, if it is for Allah, then it is obligatory upon the Imam to establish it, and if it is for the people, then it is for the people.'
ai.seo_question: What is the difference between how an Imam handles adultery versus theft according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi elucidates the Imam's dual role as both a divine witness and a judicial authority, distinguishing between Hudud (fixed penalties for God's rights) and Qisas/Dam (compensation for people's rights). It establishes that for public sins like adultery or wine consumption, the Imam's personal observation suffices for executing the penalty, reflecting his status as 'Amin Allah' (God's trustee), whereas for theft, the right is primarily private, so he intervenes to reprimand but leaves the final disposition to the victim. This distinction underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that the Imam's direct knowledge can substitute for formal testimony in specific divine rights cases.
